extracted.intended_audience: educated readers and writers of English poetry (critics and students interested in Milton and epic composition)
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical and prescriptive guidance for evaluating and composing epic poetry (illustrated via close reading of Milton's Paradise Lost, Book IV). Emphasizes descriptive technique, construction of 'machines' (plot/speeches), and character conduct in relation to scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the poem's beauties under three heads
rubrics_metrics.description: We may consider the Beauties of the Fourth Book under three Heads: (1) Pictures of Still-Life (descriptions of Eden, Paradise, Adam's bower, etc.); (2) the Machines (which comprehend the Speeches and Behaviour of the good and bad Angels); (3) the Conduct of Adam and Eve, the principal actors in the Poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tripartite frame to analyze or compose epic passages: attend separately to descriptive tableaux, to the structural/performative machinery (speeches, scene mechanics), and to the moral/psychological conduct of main characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristotle's rule: lavish ornaments on weak/unactive parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poet has observed Aristotle's Rule of lavishing all the Ornaments of Diction on the weak unactive Parts of the Fable, which are not supported by the Beauty of Sentiments and Characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply more florid, elaborate language to descriptive or 'still-life' passages rather than to active, sentiment-driven scenes. Example: descriptions of Paradise employ more ornate expression than other parts. Avoid wasting ornamentation where strong sentiment or character already supplies grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be particular in description when the scene is principal
rubrics_metrics.description: Tho the Drawings of Gardens, Rivers, Rainbows, and the like dead Pieces of Nature, are justly censured in an Heroic Poem, when they run out into an unnecessary length; the Description of Paradise would have been faulty, had not the Poet been very particular in it, not only as it is the Scene of the Principal Action, but as it is requisite to give us an Idea of that Happiness from which our first Parents fell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve lengthy, detailed description for scenes essential to the poem's action or theme. Do not indulge in long descriptive digressions unless the setting is central to understanding character/state (anti-pattern: unnecessary, prolonged landscape description that does not serve the fable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Let setting inform characters' language and thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Scarce a Speech of Adam or Eve in the whole Poem wherein the Sentiments and Allusions are not taken from this their delightful Habitation... their Thoughts are always Paradisiacal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure characters' diction, metaphors, and concerns reflect their environment and social/psychological situation (pastoral characters should speak with images drawn from woods/fields/rivers; inhabitants of Paradise should speak in paradisiacal terms). This creates coherence between scene and speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct 'machines' (speeches/behaviour) to reveal conflicting passions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Machines, which comprehend the Speeches and Behaviour of the good and bad Angels... Satan... is filled with Sentiments different from those which he discovered whilst he was in Hell. The Place inspires him with Thoughts more adapted to it: He reflects... and breaks forth into a Speech that is softened with several transient Touches of Remorse and Self-accusation: But at length he confirms himself in Impenitence...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design speeches and scene-mechanics to stage psychological conflict and moral complexity. An opening speech can move through remorse to reaffirmed vice, showing inner struggle; such gradations should be artfully raised to reveal character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use striking transformations and incidents to surprise and link episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: His bounding over the Walls of Paradise; his sitting in the Shape of a Cormorant upon the Tree of Life... his planting himself at the Ear of Eve under the form of a Toad, in order to produce vain Dreams... His starting up in his own Form is wonderfully fine, both in the Literal Description, and in the Moral which is concealed under it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ metamorphoses, disguises, and decisive incidents as devices to create agreeable surprise and to connect a series of adventures. Such devices should be chosen and described so they serve both plot cohesion and moral/significant revelation (example: Satan's various shapes link reconnaissance, temptation, and eventual exposure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose bold, noble opening speeches for crucial moments
rubrics_metrics.description: This Conflict of Passions is raised with a great deal of Art, as the opening of his Speech to the Sun is very bold and noble... This Speech is, I think, the finest that is ascribed to Satan in the whole Poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft openings of major speeches with striking imagery and tonal ambition to encapsulate the speaker's stature and inner conflict. A powerful opening can mark the finest moments of a character and set the moral/emotional register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt classical critical rules by reason, not slavishness
rubrics_metrics.description: I have not bound my self scrupulously to the Rules which any one of them has laid down upon that Art, but have taken the Liberty sometimes to join with one, and sometimes with another, and sometimes to differ from all of them, when I have thought that the Reason of the thing was on my side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use critical maxims (e.g., from Aristotle or tradition) as flexible tools. Combine, adapt, or depart from rules where reason and the demands of the poem justify it. Avoid mechanical adherence to critics when the work's necessities counsel otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep a short personal journal for self-examination (writerly practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: I would... recommend to every one of my Readers, the keeping a Journal of their Lives for one Week, and setting down punctually their whole Series of Employments during that Space of Time. This Kind of Self-Examination would give them a true State of themselves...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For writers: perform a one-week punctual record of daily activities to reveal habits, omissions, and spendings of time. Use the resulting self-knowledge to inform characterization, realistic detail, and to correct indolence or inconsistency in one's practice (practical exercise rather than formal stylistic rule).
